_README: THE ACCEPTANCE PLAN: how a run of this project is judged.  It is the
counterpart of `protocol-template.json` -- that one answers 'how is this
BUILT?', this one answers 'how do we know a run of it was RIGHT?' -- and
the onboarding skill produces both in the same pass.
The skill's job is to READ the project and FILL THIS FILE IN.  Every value
below is a fact about the project, and every one of them must come from
something the project declares -- its build system, its case list, its own
benchmark script, its documentation.  None of it may be guessed from the
outputs: a date differs from a date, and at a project's own tolerance a
one-day difference can sit inside the numeric slack, so a comparison that
INFERRED its volatile lines would call it a match.
Committed beside the protocol (gzipped, expanded on use).  One mechanism
reads it for every project: `protocolize/edd/bench_suite.py`, driven by
`python3 -m protocolize.edd.bench_cli <build_dir>`.
WHAT MUST BE TRUE BEFORE THIS FILE IS ACCEPTED.  `VerificationPlan.problems()`
is the authority and it is not advisory -- it refuses a plan that could
produce a verdict with nothing behind it.  The three that matter most:
* `summary.require_min` must be present and non-zero.  Without it a run
whose results nobody could read has zero failures, zero crashes and
zero timeouts, and reads clean.  Measured: two corpora's summaries
parsed to zero passing cases and nobody noticed, because the verdict
came from an exit code instead of a count.
* a `process` run must say `inputs.from`.  The workload runs with its cwd
in a work dir and is handed a bare input name, so a plan that does not
say what to stage describes a run that reads nothing -- and a program
that then falls through to a default branch reports a PASS for a run
that read no input at all.  Measured.
* `golden.source: none` must name a `stamp`.  Without one every origin
counts as ready, including a half-written one left by a killed
reference run.
TWO SPELLINGS, and the difference is load-bearing, exactly as in the
protocol:
* `${TREE}` -- the build tree the capture ran in.  Travels with the plan.
* ABSOLUTE -- the project's own sources and case directories.  They do
not move, and must not be rewritten.
`$` is reserved.  A literal dollar is `$$`; a bare `$` is refused.
BINDINGS, usable in any path or argument below.  A `{name}` the mechanism
does not know is left ALONE rather than emptied: an unresolved binding is
a plan asking for something that does not exist, and an empty path names
nothing.  Roots: `{target}` (the thing under test), `{tree}`, `{origin}`
(the goldens), `{results}` (this run), `{work}` (this case), `{home}`
(per-run scratch), `{jobs}`.  Per case: `{case_id}` (the corpus's own
spelling), `{input.name}`, `{input.stem}`, `{deck_rel}` (a deck's relative
path, when the cases come from a list), `{deck_stem}` (the same without its
extension), and every name declared in `produced`.
THE ORIGIN IS ONE RULE FOR EVERY PROJECT.  Run the REFERENCE instance
through this same plan and keep whatever the plan calls golden.  The
reference and the candidate therefore traverse one code path, and 'a
failed reference run captures nothing' is true by construction instead of
being a guard each project's script had to remember.
A NOTE ON CIRCLING: `golden.source: reference_run` proves the candidate
AGREES WITH THE REFERENCE, which is STABILITY, not correctness.  A project
that ships its own reference output has an external truth -- say so in
`provenance` and encode it, rather than letting a reader assume the golden
is authoritative.
_plan_version: The only version this consumer reads. A file from another version is refused, not coerced.

_README: WHAT is under test. Exactly two shapes, and which one applies is a fact
about the project, not a preference:
* `product` -- a program the build produces. `product` names it, and
the harness finds it under `<tree>/curr/bin/<product>` (or wherever
the caller passes with `-x`).
* `tree` -- a BUILD TREE, for a project whose acceptance is its own
registered test suite (a library). Its registrations live where the
build ran; the mechanism reads that directory rather than assuming.
A wrong `kind` here is not a small error: the harness used to hand every
project `<tree>/bin/<binary>`, which for a library names a path that
does not exist.
WHERE the cases come from -- the project's own declaration of its case
set. Three shapes are known, and they are told apart by what the project
HAS, never by its name:
* `one_per_dir`     -- one directory per case, a fixed-named input
inside each (see `_one_per_dir`).
* `case_list`       -- records in a file, with an INCLUDE chain and
per-record columns (see `_case_list`).
* `build_system_tests` -- the build system registered them; the set is
already in the protocol as `protocol.tests`
(see `_build_system_tests`).
The value below is ONE working example; replace this whole object with
the shape the project declares. A fourth shape may be described without
changing the mechanism, which is why this section is open.
cases.root: <absolute path to the directory holding the cases>
cases._root: Absolute, or `${TREE}`-relative when the cases are generated into the tree. It is a fact read from the project, not a guess.
cases._exclude: Directory names that are NOT cases. Omit when every directory is one.
cases._id: How a case's id is spelled: `dirname` (the directory's name) or `stem` (the input's).

input.name: {stem}.inp
input._name: The input's name inside the case directory. `{stem}` is the id in the project's own spelling.
input._id_spelling: How the id becomes the input's stem, when they differ. MEASURED: one corpus's directory `D01-00-0A` holds `d01000a.inp`, so a plan that said `{id}.inp` discovered ZERO cases. Derive it from the project's tree, and prove it covers every directory.

cases._skip_without_input: Whether a directory with no input is skipped or is an error. A project that excludes directories at all is one whose discovery requires the input.

_README: A case list: records in a file, optionally through an INCLUDE chain.
The RECORD LAYOUT is the project's, and it is read from the file --
which column is the deck, which is a selector, which is a reference
value and a tolerance. Use the WIDEST record: a corpus mixes asserted
and unasserted entries, and a narrow one would drop the criteria for
the whole corpus.
`deck_root` is the directory the deck paths are relative to, which is
NOT necessarily the list's own directory. MEASURED: one corpus's
`cases.txt` sits in `MYSTRAN_Validation/` while its decks live in
`MYSTRAN_Validation/decks/`.
_case_list.root: <absolute path to the directory holding the list>
_case_list.deck_root: <absolute path the deck paths are relative to>

_README: The build system registered the cases, so there is nothing to
enumerate here: the set is `protocol.tests`, captured from the build
system's own registry (`ctest --show-only=json-v1`). A project that
registers its tests is usually SELF-VERIFYING -- it computes its own
residuals and prints its own table -- so its `golden.source` is
`none` and its verdict comes from `self_report`.
What is staged into the case's work directory before it runs.
* `input_only` -- the case's input, nothing else.
* `case_dir`   -- every file beside it, minus `exclude_suffix`.
`case_dir` exists because a case's supporting decks and its restart
state sit BESIDE it: staging just the input produces a case that cannot
run, which then reads as a failure of the transpiler.
A `process` run MUST declare this. See the `_README` at the top.
inputs._exclude_suffix: Suffixes of files the run GENERATES, which are therefore not inputs. MEASURED: a rule rather than a fact drifts silently, so materialise it against the real directory when capturing and refuse a rule that does not match.

staging.target: <absolute path to a resource the project ships>

staging.from: <absolute path to a config it ships>

_README: HOW one case (or the whole suite) is executed. Two kinds:
* `process` -- one invocation per case. `argv` is a template.
* `suite`   -- hand the whole set to the build system's runner in one
invocation. `ctest -j {jobs} -V --timeout N` is the
build system's own spelling, the same licence the
generator has to emit `add_test`.
`exit_accept` is the project's own notion of success and is often NOT
just zero: MEASURED, one program exits 2 on a legitimate outcome.
`case_timeout_s` bounds ONE case, not the suite.
run._argv: Tokens are spelled with the bindings above. Nothing else may be hardcoded here: this field is what replaced each project's own `bench_argv`.
run._cwd: Where the run happens. `{work}` is this case's own directory; `{target}` is the tree, for a suite.
run._exit_accept: Which exit codes mean 'the run completed'. A signal death is never acceptable and is reported as CRASHED on its own.

_README: What this run WRITES, each under a name later sections refer to. The
name is the project's: MEASURED, one program writes `.F06` while its
saved goldens are `.out`, so a plan that assumed the two agree found no
artifact and reported 'no output' for all 485 cases.
An artifact nothing declares is INVISIBLE to the mechanism -- which is
how a restart chain's handover would silently have nothing to carry.
Spell them against `{work}`: a hand-written layout (e.g.
`work/{case_id}/...`) freezes the case's location at discovery time, and
a restart chain moves its prerequisites.
WHERE the thing to compare against comes from.
* `reference_run` -- captured by running the reference through this
same plan. Requires `root` and `path`.
* `none`          -- the project verifies itself (it computes and
prints its own residuals). Requires `stamp`: a file written when a
clean reference run happened, so an origin that is absent or
half-written is not treated as ready.
golden._root: The binding the goldens live under. A LITERAL path here is refused: which tree an origin belongs to is exactly what must not be guessed.
golden._path: One golden's location under `root`, as a template. MEASURED: when the cases come from a list the goldens MIRROR the deck's relative path (`{deck_stem}.out`), while the artifact is `{work}/{input.stem}.F06` -- the two names differ.

_README: Cases that must run BEFORE another, because it restarts from their
state. Both halves are required, and either alone reproduces the same
failures:
* `order` -- which case needs which, in sequence.
* `carry` -- which declared artifact is handed forward, and under the
NEXT case's own name.
MEASURED: the subsystem looks for the state under the CURRENT case's
name, so state left under its old name is simply not found -- 19 of one
corpus's 132 cases, exactly the chain members.
Prerequisites and the final case share ONE work directory (that corpus's
database files must reside together), and only the FINAL case is judged:
a prerequisite's golden describes a different deck.
A project with no such dependency leaves `order` empty.
PROVENANCE MATTERS. One corpus's 19 chains could not be derived from
anything in its tree -- id succession, shipped restart state, the
project's own prose, and archive membership were each measured and none
reproduces the table -- so they travel as CATALOGUED data and say so.
Do not fit a rule to the rows you can see: it passes today and breaks on
the project's next case.
chains._order: case id -> the ids that must run before it, in order.
chains._carry: Which declared artifact (a name from `produced`) is handed forward. It must be one the plan declares: a carry rule naming an artifact that does not exist hands forward nothing.

report._repeats: How many times to run, to show the verdict is DETERMINISTIC. Report-only: it is NEVER a gate, because turning a toolchain's floating-point non-determinism into a failure manufactures false positives. Several runs are needed to STORE a metric reference -- a single reading is not a reference.

_README: The plan's own verdict. Both halves are required for a meaningful one.
`require_zero` names the verdicts that must not occur.
`require_min` is the conjunct that makes the rest mean anything: a run
whose results never reached the reader has every count at zero, so
without a floor the emptiest possible run is the greenest. A plan with
no `require_min` is REFUSED.

provenance: Say what the golden PROVES. `reference_run` proves the candidate agrees with the reference -- stability, not correctness. A project that ships its own reference output has an external truth: name it and encode it.
comment: onboarded from <the directory this was captured from>

_README: The project's own preparation: what its programs need in order to RUN.
A CLOSED vocabulary -- an op the mechanism does not perform is refused,
never ignored, because a skipped preparation is a run that cannot start
and must not report a difference as if it had.
* `env`        -- set a variable for the run.
* `mkdir`      -- create a directory.
* `symlink`    -- link a resource the project ships.
* `substitute` -- copy a file the project ships, with literal
replacements. `required: true` (the default) means a
search text that is ABSENT is a hard error: the file
is shipped, so a mismatch is silent by nature.
* `alias`      -- make each staged file reachable under its UPPERCASE
name too. Some projects open a file under a spelling
they do not ship (`rscards` opened as `RSCARDS`);
without it the run reads nothing and reports no
error of its own.
The `staging` array above is one op of each kind, each holding
placeholders to replace. A project that needs none declares none.
MEASURED: without one corpus's preparation its program exits 0 and
writes NOTHING, and all 132 cases report 'no output' -- which reads as a
broken transpiler, not as a missing preparation.
WHAT must be true of a case's outcome. An assertion kind the mechanism
does not run is REFUSED, never skipped: a skipped assertion is a
criterion nobody applied, which reads exactly like one that passed.
Kinds:
* `artifact`        -- a declared artifact exists (set `non_empty` too
when an empty one must not count).
* `text_lockstep`   -- line by line against the golden, after dropping
the volatile lines, with a numeric tolerance.
* `field_assertion` -- a per-table COLUMN model: which token positions
of each table are physical quantities. Use this
when the project prints TABLES.  It is a table
and not a pattern list because a DERIVED column
(a principal-stress ANGLE) must be skipped while
the real stresses ON ITS ROW are still compared
-- 'drop the line' would stop comparing those.
* `self_report`     -- read the project's own summary and apply ITS
verdict. Requires `require_min` (a floor: 5,444,421
checks is a magnitude, and a reader that found
*a* table would pass a run that did a fraction of
the work) and `require_zero`.
* `metric`          -- a measured number against a stored reference.
The two arrays above are one `artifact` and one `text_lockstep`.  A
project whose output is tables replaces the second with a
`field_assertion` shaped like the one under `_field_assertion`; a project
that verifies itself uses a `self_report` like the one under
`_self_report`.
THE TOLERANCE AND THE VOLATILE-LINE LIST ARE THE PROJECT'S.  Read them
from the file that states them and pass it as `declaration=`; never
search for it, because a search that widened until it found something
would find a NEIGHBOUR's.
`drop` holds volatile-line REGEXES -- lines that legitimately differ
between two runs of the same thing (timestamps, host, elapsed).  Do not
invent them: a list widened by hand drops lines the project never said
were volatile, which is a comparison that accepts a difference.
`rtol`/`atol` are how much numeric slack the project's PHYSICS allows.
They are two real measurements, not one default copied everywhere.
Which token positions of each table are PHYSICAL QUANTITIES.
`titles` are the table's own headings with all whitespace removed, as
the project prints them (a project that spaces a title out letter by
letter is matched unspaced).
Each row rule names the SHAPE it applies to -- `first_eq`, `first_int`,
`second_int`, `n_tokens` -- and the `fields` it reads.  A row matching
no rule is still COMPARED, by the ordinary numeric comparison:
treating it as 'not declared, therefore not judged' would turn every
shape the model forgot into a region nobody checks.
`near_zero` is the magnitude below which a component is a THEORETICAL
ZERO whose relative error is meaningless (a free-expansion thermal
deck is full of them): such a component is compared absolutely, while
a real magnitude is still held to `rtol`.
`by_elemtype` gives some element types their own row shapes and every
other type the `''` DEFAULT.
model.elemtype_line: \\bF O R E L E M E N T T Y P E (.+)

_self_report._section_pattern: The project's own section headings, so the counts are attributed to the right section. A heading that does not match ENDS attribution, rather than letting one section's totals be summed into another's.
_self_report._require_min: The floor. Measured: one suite reports 5,444,421 checks in one section and 315,872 in another, and a reader that found *a* table would pass a run that did a fraction of the work.
